Field surveys across sub-Saharan Africa indicate that the African giant shrew (Crocidura olivieri) reaches a maximum adult body mass of approximately 60 grams [Wwi = approximately 60 grams], a figure consistent with measurements taken from populations in Nigeria where individuals typically range from 37 to 65 grams. Newborn pups are surprisingly small for such a large-bodied shrew, with a neonatal wet weight of just 4.9 grams [Wwb = 4.9 grams], a value extrapolated from data on the closely related Crocidura russula after accounting for differences in adult size. This altricial neonate, born hairless and with closed eyes, undergoes a period of rapid mass gain during the suckling stage, ultimately reaching a weaning mass of 40.3 grams [Wwx = 40.3 grams] when nutritional independence begins. The trajectory from a birth mass of under five grams to an adult body mass that is over twelve times larger underscores the intensity of early postnatal growth in this species, which is thought to be an adaptation to high predation pressure in its savanna and forest-edge habitats.

Reproductive output in Crocidura olivieri has been estimated through comparisons with the better-studied congener Crocidura russula. Females are believed to produce litters of four pups [N_R_i = litters of four pups], with approximately three and a half litters occurring annually [F_R_i = approximately three and a half litters occurring annually], yielding a substantial yearly reproductive rate. Gestation is brief and occurs under the thermoneutral conditions typical of the species' resting metabolism, lasting 35 days [tg = 35 days] at a body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. The postpartum pups remain entirely dependent on maternal milk for the first several weeks, and weaning—marked by the cessation of lactation and the transition to solid food—takes place at 45 days after birth [tx = 45 days after birth] under the same thermal regime of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This relatively short period of maternal investment is characteristic of many shrew species, which prioritize rapid development and early independence to maximize lifetime reproductive success in unpredictable environments.

Basal metabolic rate in Crocidura olivieri has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], yielding a resting oxygen consumption of 58.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 58.4 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value reflects the high metabolic demands typical of the Soricidae, a family renowned for its elevated mass-specific metabolic rates relative to other eutherian mammals of comparable size. The shrew's daily energetic costs of tissue upkeep are considerable, necessitating a near-continuous foraging strategy and a diet dominated by invertebrates with high energy density. Field observations corroborate this physiological trait, as individuals have been documented consuming up to twice their own body mass in prey each day, a behavioral adaptation that directly supports the elevated resting metabolic rate measured at thermoneutrality.

Sexual maturation in the African giant shrew occurs relatively late for a mammal of its body size, with puberty attained at 150 days after birth [tp = 150 days after birth] under the normal thermal conditions of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This delay likely reflects the considerable time required to reach the asymptotic adult mass of approximately 60 grams from the much smaller weaning weight. The onset of gametogenesis and the first oestrous cycle mark the transition from a weaned juvenile to a reproductively viable adult capable of contributing to the next generation. In contrast to many smaller shrew species that mature within a few weeks, the longer pubertal timeline of Crocidura olivieri appears to be an allometric consequence of its larger body size, with field data from Nigerian populations supporting the existence of a prolonged sub-adult phase during which individuals continue to develop before initiating breeding activity.

Longevity records for Crocidura olivieri remain sparse, but extrapolations based on the life history of Crocidura russula suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years] under the optimal thermal conditions of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C] typical of a resting, non-stressed individual. When converted into daily units, this span represents roughly 1461 days, a duration that affords the species multiple breeding seasons given its annual reproductive output. The life history strategy of this shrew, characterized by modest longevity relative to larger mammals yet high fecundity and rapid juvenile development, aligns with a classic r-selected demographic profile common among small insectivores occupying temporally variable habitats. Comparative analyses with other members of the genus Crocidura indicate that variation in lifespan is tightly linked to both body mass and basal metabolic rate, with the high energetic throughput of Crocidura olivieri likely contributing to accelerated senescence relative to similarly-sized rodents.
